Zamboni N.lab_name: Zamboni Group, Institute of Molecular Systems Biology, ETH Zurich (Zurich, Switzerland)
Zamboni N.role: Group leader at ETH Zurich's Institute of Molecular Systems Biology who develops mass spectrometry methods to measure hundreds of metabolites at once, used in many collaborations on cell metabolism
Zamboni N.sub: Group leader, Institute of Molecular Systems Biology, ETH Zurich (since 2005) · postdoc, Stanford Genome Technology Center (2004) · PhD, Institute of Biotechnology, ETH Zurich, Jay Bailey group (2003)
story: Nicola Zamboni is a co-author of two Atlas studies that measured cell metabolism. GEI2016 tracked metabolites and proteins in activated human T cells and found that the amino acid L-arginine drops sharply after activation; raising L-arginine pushed the cells toward oxidative metabolism, made them live longer and improved their anti-tumor activity in a mouse model. DEM2026 found that losing the enzyme IDH3A in leukemic stem cells of acute myeloid leukemia slows the citric acid cycle and raises citrate, which switches on AMPK, turns down mTORC1 and makes the cells more sensitive to the drug venetoclax.

In both studies the key data came from metabolomics, the large-scale measurement of small molecules in cells. Zamboni earned a PhD at ETH Zurich in 2003 in the group of Jay Bailey at the Institute of Biotechnology, working on metabolic engineering and 13C flux analysis, a method that follows carbon atoms from a labelled nutrient to see which metabolic routes a cell uses. A postdoc at the Stanford Genome Technology Center from 2004 added mass spectrometry and metabolomics in eukaryotic cells.

Zamboni returned to ETH Zurich in 2005 and leads a group at the Institute of Molecular Systems Biology. The lab builds mass spectrometry, metabolomics and stable-isotope tracer methods, together with software for analysing the data, to measure how whole metabolic networks respond inside living cells. More than 30 papers are shared with Uwe Sauer, a systems biologist at the same institute, and many others are collaborations in microbiology, immunology, aging and cancer biology.
